Council Tables Annexation, Rezone Request
Attendees listen at last night’s Shelbyville Common Council meeting. | photo by JACK BOYCE
The Shelbyville Common Council last night voted to table an annexation and rezoning request involving more than 400 acres east of the Interstate 74–State Road 44 interchange, delaying action on land targeted for a potential data center campus until its next meeting on Feb. 18. The request, tied to interest from Prologis, would bring the largely agricultural property into city limits and rezone it as a first step toward evaluating a multiphase data center development. Council members cited the need for additional time and due diligence following an unfavorable recommendation from the Plan Commission and extensive public concern. No vote was taken on the merits of the proposal itself, and the matter will return to the council for further consideration next month. Look for additional reporting in an upcoming edition.
Golden Bears Win on Senior Night
Shelbyville High School senior basketball players are recognized prior to last night’s game. Top left, then clockwise: Hannah Baker, escorted by Kyle Baker and Leslie Baker; Maddy Jones escorted by J.R. and Brittany Jones; Alivia Lee, escorted by Clint and Kelly Lee; Avery Keller, escorted by Suzette Keller; Reese Fortune, escorted by Craig and Jennifer Fortune; and Savannah Collins, escorted by Brock and Kylonda Clark. | photos by KRISTIAAN RAWLINGS
On Senior Night last night, the Shelbyville High School girls basketball team built an early cushion and held off a late push to defeat Whiteland, 65-53, improving to 11-8 on the season while Whiteland fell to 5-15. The Golden Bears honored seniors Hannah Baker, Maddy Jones, Savannah Collins, Alivia Lee, Reese Fortune and Avery Keller prior to tipoff, with five of the six seniors in the starting lineup and all seeing action. Shelbyville scored the game’s first 14 points and led 14-5 after one quarter, but Whiteland steadily chipped away, cutting the margin to 29-22 at halftime and 47-41 after three. The Bears opened the fourth quarter by working the ball around the perimeter for nearly 30 seconds before Jayla Ash knocked down a three to push the lead back to nine. Whiteland responded, but Shelbyville controlled the tempo down the stretch, burning clock and forcing fouls late to seal the win. Ash led the Bears with 25 points, Collins added 16, Jones scored 8, Baker with 7, Melia Cartwright with 5 and Kiah Pandoli with 2. The Golden Bears host Delta on Saturday afternoon.

NOTEBOOK:
The Shelby County Council gave the go-ahead Tuesday for Prosecutor Brad Landwerlen to obtain expanded data storage. Landwerlen briefed the council regarding the growing strain digital evidence is placing on law enforcement and court systems. He cited the rapid expansion of police body-camera footage and cellphone extractions that must be stored, reviewed and redacted for discovery. Landwerlen said prosecutors and staff now routinely spend hours uploading single files and must maintain both original and redacted copies of evidence, sometimes from multiple officers’ body cameras, for a single incident, particularly when statements reference prior arrests or include sensitive material that must be redacted. The proposed contract is with Axon, which would provide unlimited digital evidence storage along with tools for automated transcription, translation, AI-generated case summaries and advanced redaction, which could reduce the need to hire additional staff while improving efficiency and security. The system would also allow controlled, view-only access to sensitive evidence by defense attorneys, preventing downloads or redistribution and would create an audit trail of all access. County IT Director John Johnson said the county’s current infrastructure is not equipped to handle the volume of data prosecutors now generate and confirmed he would cover half the annual cost. The council gave conditional approval to move forward, pending final allocation of funding, with the total annual cost set at $25,566, split evenly between the Prosecutor’s Office and county IT.
Shelbyville Fire Chief Doug Lutes provided an update to the Shelby County Council on a recently approved interlocal agreement that allows county-run dispatch to send the Edinburgh Fire Department to provide ambulance service in a portion of southwestern Shelby County to improve response times. Lutes said the agreement formalizes practices already used informally and targets an area where Shelbyville units can face 15 to 20 minute response times, even with lights and sirens. Under the agreement, Shelbyville will continue to respond to all calls, but Edinburgh units, which are often able to arrive within five minutes, may handle incidents if they arrive first and can provide equal or higher levels of care, including advanced life support when available. Lutes estimated the area accounts for fewer than 50 calls annually and emphasized the goal is faster care for patients while keeping Shelbyville ambulances available in the county.
The Shelby County Council reelected Brett Haacker as president on a 4-3 vote, with Jeremy Ruble receiving three votes. Leigh Langkabel was reelected vice president, 4-3, with Kyle Barlow receiving three votes.
Shelby County residents can receive free help navigating recent tax changes, including increases to the standard deduction and child tax credit, a senior bonus, and new deductions for tips, new car loan interest and required overtime, through the VITA program offered by Purdue Extension - Shelby County. Sponsored by the Internal Revenue Service, Volunteer Income Tax Assistance (VITA) provides accurate, no-cost tax preparation by IRS-certified volunteers for individuals and families with low to moderate incomes. VITA will be offered Saturdays from Feb. 7 through April 4 at Purdue Extension - Shelby County, 20 W. Polk St., Suite 201, Shelbyville. For more information, call 317-392-6460.
A single-vehicle crash occurred Tuesday night at the intersection of East Washington and North Harrison streets. A gray Ford Focus left the roadway while making a right turn and struck a curb; the driver was found to be intoxicated and was arrested. The vehicle was towed from the scene.
Authorities have identified the victim in a fatal Delaware County burning as 58-year-old Michael D. Greer of Shelbyville, according to investigators. Greer was found inside a burning vehicle in a rural area of Delaware County in mid-December, with evidence indicating he was alive when the fire was set. Multiple suspects have since been charged in the case, including two men accused of kidnapping Greer in Indianapolis and transporting him to Delaware County, where the vehicle was set on fire, WTHR reported.

Again, thank you so much for your loyal support of this endeavor. - Kristiaan Rawlings, Ph.D.HOOSIER NEWS: The Indiana Senate on Tuesday approved a bill tightening school cellphone restrictions, sending the measure to the House after a divided vote and lengthy debate. The proposal would require public schools to adopt either a complete ban on student devices or a secure storage policy keeping phones inaccessible throughout the school day, expanding current limits that apply only during instructional time. Opponents raised concerns about safety, costs and enforcement, while supporters argued phone-free schools improve learning and student well-being. State Sen. Jean Leising (R-Oldenburg) was one of the 19 to oppose, while 28 voted in favor. (IBJ)

This Day in Shelby County History
Local headlines reported on or around this date in Shelby County history. Selections are curated by The Addison Times from Shelby County Public Library Genealogy Department materials.
2006: The late Carol Finkel received the Indiana Music Educators Association’s 2006 Outstanding Hoosier Musician. “Carol Finkel was the type of person who never would accept praise or accolades for what she did. She would have none of it when she was alive, so my chance to honor her for all she did has finally arrived,” Russell Smith, a nominator, said. Other nominators for Finkel came from Joel Kenemore, LuAnn Mason, Wayne Rose, Steven Lancaster, Don Wickizer, Daniel Wickizer, Donna Holland, Mark Moore and Loretta Eckstein.
1996: ShelbyNet, owned by Bill Pandak, was set to open within days, providing Shelbyville’s first local internet connection. Up to that point, internet users had to dial long-distance to Indianapolis. More than 75 people had already subscribed to ShelbyNet. Pandak said he hoped for up to 500 subscribers.
1986: Concrete window sills were placed on the new addition to the south wing of Shelbyville High School. The new area would house science and special education classrooms.
1976: The Northwestern Consolidated School District became the first in Shelby County to provide one-way transportation for kindergarten students, a decision made following a four-hour school board meeting.
1966: Nancy Main, Hendricks Township, a senior at Southwestern High School, was chosen as Shelby County Corn Queen. Other finalists were Charlotte Engle, Shirley Rick, Linda Miller, Charlotte Ellison, Diane Keaton and Sherri Barlow.
1956: Louis Hamner won the Mt. Auburn school “1955 Predictions Contest” for having made the highest percentage of correct events.
The Parks Belk department store prepared to open on Public Square. The building, formerly Cahn’s Smith, had closed due to fire. Parks Belk was renovating the front and installing blue-tinted tile.
1946: Three returned servicemen, Dr. D.B. Silbert, J.M. McKeand and John Wetnight, spoke at the Kiwanis Club meeting.
1936: A local piano tuner who was driving drunk ran into the city police car occupied by Officer Walter Winton. The piano tuner drove away and Winton chase him around the downtown area before making the arrest. Since Mayor Webb was home due to a recent heart attack, the piano tuner sat in jail while officers looked for a judge pro tem.
1926: Board members of First Christian Church announced the church had become debt-free in 1925. Total membership of the church was 671. Rev. T.J. Wilson reported he had conducted 18 funerals, 23 marriages and made 207 pastoral visits.
1916: A miniature lake stood at the intersection of Harrison and West Jackson, causing numerous downtown business owners and workers to be late to work. The lake had been caused by manholes overflowing at the intersection. “Women who came along the street were made to detour down Jackson Street and cross on a very dangerous piece of ice,” The Republican said. The paper said one business had suggested to another that they should swim across. “No siree,” the other reportedly said. “I’se a Methodist, not a Baptist.”

OBITUARIES
Charles T. Bate, 93, of Indianapolis, Indiana, passed away on January 15, 2026. He was born on November 14, 1932, in Muncie, Indiana, to parents, Thomas E. Bate and Vina Florence (Jackson) Bate.
Charles graduated from Butler University in 1955 and Indiana University Law School in 1962. He was a Trustee Emeritus at Anderson University, Trustee at Warner Pacific College, and founding member of the Indiana Trial Lawyers Association. His other accomplishments and recognitions are too many to mention. His greatest love of lawyering was helping others through their toughest times.
He was extremely active in the Church of God movement. He helped form and start many churches and programs throughout his life. Even after retirement, he started the Stephen Ministry and was an Elder at the Church at the Crossing where he started a bereavement program and also taught Kindergarten.
His greatest love was for his wife, Barbara, of 70 plus years of marriage. He always talked about what a blessing it was to have such a wife. “Together Forever.” He was most proud of being a son, husband, father, grandfather, and great-grandfather. These are the things he cherished. He had a motto to live by. It was HIDTWIC, “Have I done today what I could.” He always did. His favorite song was “It Is Well With My Soul.”
Charles is survived by his loving wife, Barbara Kay (Dailey) Bate; sons, Charles “Chuck” (Karen) Bate, Gregory (Cheri) Bate, and Jeffrey (Leslie) Bate; grandchildren, Ashley, Danielle, Tyler, Joshua, Samuel, Taylor, Haley and Grace. He also had nine (9) great-grandchildren. There will be a Celebration of Life in the future. Memorial contributions in his name may be made to The Church at the Crossing, 9111 Haverstick Rd, Indianapolis, IN 46240.
